open-question.question: The Antigravity slot values are to be rewritten from a hands-on check against the installed agy. Where is that check recorded so a later editor can tell what each value was written against: in the comment above each value in the host definition, in the milestone's decisions only, as a repeatable script kept in the repository, or nowhere beyond the values themselves?
open-question.alternative: Recorded in the Antigravity host definition, per value: the comment above each Antigravity slot value in scripts/hosts/antigravity/settings.toml names the agy version the value was checked against and the observed behaviour it rests on (what dispatch, waiting, continuing an agent, or the context file was seen to do). No separate file, script, or CLAUDE.md entry carries the check. The record sits at the exact place an editor changing a value reads, and it extends the existing convention that each slot comment says why this host's value is what it is, so a value written from observation and one written by inference are told apart at a glance. The version is repeated across every Antigravity comment and nothing checks it, so a value edited later without a re-check keeps a stamp that now overclaims, and a newer agy leaves every stamp silently stale; where a value ends up held in a file rather than inline is a condition on whether a comment can sit above it at all (the inline-versus-file assignment and the file-backed binding form are sibling questions).

Recorded in the Antigravity host definition, once: a single block in the header comment of scripts/hosts/antigravity/settings.toml names the agy version and date of the check and lists what was observed; the per-value comments state only what each value describes and why, in mechanism terms, with no version. A later re-check updates one block rather than every comment, and the definition still carries its own evidence where an editor of it looks first. The stamp covers the whole definition, so a single value edited afterwards without a re-check still reads as checked; an editor must connect a value to the header list by hand rather than seeing its basis beside it.

Recorded in this milestone's directory only: the check's agy version and each observation the values rest on are written out deliberately in the milestone's own record (its Decisions and the completing task's Verified entry in TASKS_DONE.md); the host definition's comments keep describing each value in mechanism terms with no version or reference to the check. Adds nothing to maintain: the record is a committed, dated snapshot that never claims to be current, and git blame on a value leads to the milestone commits that wrote it. An editor reading settings.toml sees no sign that a value was observed or against which agy, and must know to dig through history to find it; the milestone files are not where host-definition editors look.

Recorded in CLAUDE.md: the rewritten "Host wording differences are named slots" invariant states that the Antigravity values were written from a hands-on check, names the agy version, and summarises the observed mechanisms they rest on; the host definition's comments carry no version. CLAUDE.md is already the home of rationale and is read at the start of every session, and today's invariant already explains why the Antigravity value is what it is, so the replacement explanation lands where the old one stood. Puts a volatile tool version and behaviour facts into the invariants file, which is meant to hold lasting design decisions, and separates the evidence from the values it covers so the two can drift apart unnoticed.

Recorded as an executable probe kept in the repository (under scripts/): it runs the installed agy's version, help, and agent-listing commands and checks the strings the Antigravity values rely on, and each Antigravity slot comment points at it; the parts of the check it cannot automate are noted in the script beside the commands. A re-check after an agy update is one command rather than a manual investigation, and the evidence can be reproduced rather than taken on trust. Only the static facts (version, flags, help strings, agent listing) are scriptable; dispatch, waiting, and continuing an agent need a live model session that is nondeterministic, billed, and logged in, so the script proves the least important part; it cannot run in CI where agy is absent, adds an untested script to scripts/, and goes stale as silently as a comment.

Not recorded anywhere deliberately: the rewritten values stand on their own, their comments describe each mechanism and why the value is what it is with no version or reference to the check, and the only trace is whatever the routine completion entry and commit history happen to hold. Makes no claim that can go stale, matches how the Codex values are recorded today (their comments cite the mechanism and no version), and adds no artifact to keep in step with agy. A later editor cannot tell what agy the values were written against or whether a value was observed rather than inferred, which is the very uncertainty that left the Antigravity values unchecked until this milestone.

open-question.question: A text file conventionally ends with a newline while an inline TOML slot value does not. When a file-backed slot value is substituted into a core/ file, are its bytes used verbatim, or is trailing whitespace normalised, and by what rule?
open-question.alternative: The build removes every trailing whitespace character (all final newlines, spaces, and tabs) from a file-backed value before substituting it, keeping leading whitespace and interior bytes verbatim. A value that must end in whitespace cannot be file-backed and stays inline in settings.toml. The most forgiving rule: however an editor or a stray keystroke leaves the end of the file, the rendered tree is the same, so the file ending can never introduce a blank line or a drift diff into a host tree, and the rule matches how the inline multi-line values are written today (closing ''' straight after the last word). A slot whose value legitimately ends in whitespace — today's Codex prompt-opener values end in "\n\n" — can never move to a file, so the two forms are no longer equivalent and the rule constrains which slots may be file-backed, which is the Inline versus file assignment question's to settle; whether this matters depends on that outcome.

The build reads a file-backed value as UTF-8 text and removes exactly one trailing line ending (a final "
", or "
") if the file ends with one, keeping every other byte as written, earlier trailing newlines and spaces included; a file with no final newline is used as it stands. No check is added for the file's ending. Files can follow the ordinary text-file convention editors and tools enforce, while a value whose meaning needs trailing whitespace (such as the Codex prompt-opener values that today end in "

" inline) can still be held in a file by writing one extra newline, so the file form can carry any value the inline form can and the rule is one sentence long. The file's bytes and the substituted bytes differ by one invisible character, so a reader must know the rule to tell what a file with two final newlines yields, and a value meant to end in exactly one newline needs a file ending in two, which looks like a mistake and invites someone to "fix" it.

The build removes leading and trailing whitespace (blank lines and spaces at both ends) from a file-backed value, keeping interior bytes verbatim, so a file may open or close with blank lines or a comment-free margin. A value that must begin or end in whitespace stays inline. Gives the file author the most freedom in layout — a blank first line, trailing blank lines, any final newline — with one symmetric rule that is easy to state and test. Silently discards leading whitespace too, which no value needs stripped today and which an indented or newline-prefixed value would rely on, so it widens the set of values the file form cannot carry beyond the trailing-whitespace case for no gain the trailing-only rules lack; whether that set matters again depends on the Inline versus file assignment outcome.

The build substitutes a file-backed value's bytes exactly as read, with no normalisation, and the definition loader refuses a value file whose last byte is a newline (failing the build with a message naming the file), so a value file must be saved without a final newline; a value that needs trailing whitespace other than a newline can still be file-backed. What the file holds is exactly what lands in the tree, with no hidden rule for a reader to learn, and a stray final newline is caught at build time rather than surfacing as an unexplained blank line in a rendered host tree. Fights the near-universal convention that text files end in a newline: many editors, formatters, and git's "No newline at end of file" warning push the other way, so value files are awkward to edit and the refusal will fire routinely; and a value that must end in a newline (the Codex prompt openers) cannot be file-backed at all.

The build substitutes a file-backed value's bytes exactly as read, with no normalisation and no check of the file's ending; keeping a value file free of an unwanted final newline is left to whoever edits it. The least build code and the simplest contract: the file is the value, every value the inline form can express (trailing "\n\n" included) can be expressed in a file, and nothing is ever altered behind the author's back. Any editor that appends the conventional final newline silently changes the rendered tree — an extra line break after a paragraph slot, or a broken sentence where a slot sits mid-line — and the drift gate does not catch it, because the rebuilt tree is what gets committed; the error surfaces only in review of the rendered diff, if at all.

open-question.question: The Claude Code sourcing decision covers only the two new slots, and the Codex decision keeps the eight existing Codex values unless the run contradicts one. The existing Claude Code ALTERNATIVES_CONCURRENCY value still describes two wait mechanisms (a blocking dispatch form and a wake-up form) and names neither as this host's own. Are the eight existing Claude Code values, that two-armed paragraph in particular, rewritten to the single mechanism the hands-on claude check observes, or kept as written?
open-question.alternative: None of the eight existing Claude Code values is re-checked or rewritten. The two-armed ALTERNATIVES_CONCURRENCY paragraph ("Where it offers a blocking dispatch form ... Where it offers no blocking form ... Both arms write the same blocks") and its comment ("names the wait by the agent tool's capability rather than by one primitive") stay character for character. The other seven (CONTEXT_FILE, the two dispatch values, the two empty prompt-instruction values, and the AGENT_TOOL and ALTERNATIVES_AGENT values that the slots decision retires anyway) are moved into their slot files unchanged. The hands-on claude check feeds only the two new slots. The smallest change, and it stays inside the scope the sourcing decisions recorded: the Claude Code check covers only the new slots, so no existing value's wording moves and the Claude Code tree's diff comes only from the new slots and the file move. The Claude Code tree keeps describing two wait mechanisms and naming neither as its own, which goes against the goal's "each host's tree describes only its own mechanism". The new repair value, lifted from the Claude Code arm only, would sit beside a wait paragraph that still branches. Its repair-wait sentence points back at "the paragraph opening this step", so it would be answering a branch that paragraph never settles.

ALTERNATIVES_CONCURRENCY alone is rewritten to the one wait mechanism the hands-on claude check observes. Where the check finds the agent tool offering both a blocking form and a background form, the value prescribes one as this host's own and drops the other arm, the "Both arms" closing sentence, and the capability wording of its comment. The other seven values are not re-checked and stay as written apart from the move into slot files. It fixes the one existing Claude Code value that is actually capability-conditional, so the Claude Code tree describes a single wait and agrees with the single-arm repair value. The other values already name one mechanism (`Agent` with `subagent_type`, the `cairn:` names, `CLAUDE.md`), so re-checking them adds nothing. It goes beyond the recorded sourcing decision, which kept existing values out of the Claude Code check, and the CLAUDE.md invariant describing the value as one capability-conditional paragraph must be rewritten to match. The Agent tool in this environment offers both forms (`run_in_background` defaults to background), so a single arm commits the host to one of them. The dropped fallback is lost for any Claude Code version or setting where that form is missing.

The hands-on claude check also covers the eight existing Claude Code values, mirroring the Codex rule. Each is kept as written unless the check contradicts it, and the two-armed ALTERNATIVES_CONCURRENCY paragraph counts as not contradicted as long as one of its arms matches what the check observes. Unless the check finds neither arm, it therefore stays two-armed. One symmetric rule across Claude Code and Codex: every existing value is validated against the installed binary, and none is reworded unless the evidence demands it, which keeps churn to what the check proves wrong. The check costs more, and it almost certainly leaves the two-armed paragraph standing, because a paragraph covering both forms is rarely "contradicted". The Claude Code tree keeps naming no wait mechanism as its own, against the goal, and the single-arm repair value still sits beside a branching wait paragraph.

The hands-on claude check covers all eight existing Claude Code values. ALTERNATIVES_CONCURRENCY is rewritten to the single observed wait mechanism without conditions (one arm prescribed as this host's own if both forms are available), with its comment rewritten to match. The other seven are kept as written unless the check contradicts one. The Claude Code tree describes one wait and one repair mechanism, consistent with the goal and the new repair slot. Every existing value is also checked against the installed claude by the same contradiction rule the Codex values follow, so no wrong value survives unnoticed. It costs the most of the targeted options. The claude check grows from four points to every existing value, and this option takes on both the rewrite of the CLAUDE.md invariant and the single-arm commitment, with the fallback lost where the prescribed form is missing.

All eight existing Claude Code values and their comments are re-authored from the hands-on claude check, the same way the Antigravity values are rewritten, whether or not the check contradicts them. ALTERNATIVES_CONCURRENCY becomes a single-arm paragraph, and the others are reworded to describe what the check observed, in phrasing consistent with the two new slots. Every Claude Code value and comment is written against one observed run in one consistent voice, so each slot file can be traced to the same evidence and reads uniformly beside the new repair value. It churns wording that is already single-mechanism and correct (`CLAUDE.md`, the `Agent`/`subagent_type` dispatch sentences, the empty prompt-instruction values). That widens the diff of every Claude Code skill rendering those slots for no behavioural gain and departs furthest from the recorded scope of the Claude Code check.

open-question.question: The hands-on agy check may contradict Antigravity facts held outside any slot value and outside docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md: the plugin_root literal .agents/plugins/cairn (the installed copy on this machine lives under ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn), the README template's install path and its /init instruction, and the plugin.json template. When the check contradicts one of these, is it corrected in this milestone, or recorded and left for a later one?
open-question.alternative: Every non-slot Antigravity fact the hands-on agy check contradicts is corrected in this milestone, whatever the correction takes: the plugin_root literal in scripts/hosts/antigravity/settings.toml, the README template's install path and mkdir/curl lines (which must name the same location as plugin_root), the README's /init sentence beyond the AGENTS.md rewording already decided, and the plugin.json template's schema and fields. Where a correct value cannot be expressed through the existing settings keys and templates, the build is changed as far as the correction needs. The Antigravity tree leaves this milestone right end to end, so the slot values rewritten from the agy check actually work: every {{PLUGIN_ROOT}} path they and the rest of the tree carry (the open-question tool calls, and the agent file path a generic-subagent fallback would read) resolves where agy really loads the plugin, and the install instructions a user follows produce that layout. Scope can grow past what the goal names (slot values and docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md) at an unknown size: a plugin_root change re-renders every Antigravity runtime file that references the plugin root, and if agy really loads plugins from a per-user location such as ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn installed through agy plugin import or install, the install section changes model entirely and may need build support the milestone never planned.

A contradicted non-slot fact is corrected in this milestone when the correction is an edit to an existing settings value or template: the plugin_root string together with the README install path that must match it, the README's /init sentence, and the plugin.json template's fields. A contradiction whose correction would need a new settings key, a new template kind the build does not render today, or a change to build code is left as it stands and recorded under the milestone's Out of Scope, naming the fact and what agy showed. The common corrections, a different path string, a reworded sentence, a manifest field, land at the cost of a value or template edit, while the build's schema and code change only as far as the goal already names (file-backed slots), the same bound the recorded agent-loading decision draws. The split follows how a fix is built rather than how much it matters, so the most consequential contradiction, where agy actually loads the plugin from, may be exactly the one deferred while cosmetic ones are fixed, leaving the tree's slot values pointing through a plugin root known to be wrong; how the deferral is recorded beside the check itself depends on the record form the hands-on check record question settles.

No non-slot Antigravity fact is changed in this milestone, whatever the agy check shows: the plugin_root literal, the README install path and /init sentence (beyond the AGENTS.md rewording already decided), and the plugin.json template stay as they are. Each contradiction the check finds is recorded under the milestone's Out of Scope, naming the fact and what agy showed, for a later milestone to correct. The milestone stays exactly the size its goal names, rewriting slot values and the docs page from the check without letting the check reopen the plugin's install model, and the later milestone that takes the corrections up starts from a written list rather than a rediscovery. The milestone knowingly ships an Antigravity tree whose install instructions or plugin root may be wrong, so the slot values it carefully rewrites from a hands-on check can still fail in practice wherever they reach a {{PLUGIN_ROOT}} path, and the README sentence already being edited for the context file keeps any wrong command it carries; how the deferral is recorded beside the check itself depends on the record form the hands-on check record question settles.

open-question.question: The sourcing decisions now require hands-on checks against the installed claude and codex as well as against agy. Does whatever record form is chosen for the Antigravity check (the Hands-on check record question) apply in the same form to the Claude Code and Codex checks, or is only the Antigravity check recorded?
open-question.alternative: Host coverage: only the Antigravity check is recorded, in whatever form the Hands-on check record question settles. The hands-on claude and codex checks leave no record beyond the slot values they produce and the existing comments above them, which keep their current what-and-why shape. Puts the record where the evidence gap actually was: the Antigravity values have never been written from a check of Antigravity and are being rewritten wholesale, while the Claude Code values are lifted from existing wording kept unless contradicted and the eight existing Codex values are not re-checked at all, so recording only Antigravity adds the least to maintain. The new Claude Code and Codex repair values (the follow-up to a finished agent, the fresh re-dispatch, the repair wait) are also written from a hands-on run, and a later editor cannot tell what installed version they were observed against or that they were checked at all, so the three host definitions carry unequal provenance for values of the same kind; if the sibling settles on recording nowhere, this option and the others coincide.

Host coverage: all three checks are recorded. Form: the same form the Hands-on check record question settles for Antigravity, applied unchanged to Claude Code and Codex. Value scope: each host's record covers exactly the values its check sourced or confirmed (for Codex, the new repair values and any existing value the run contradicted; for Claude Code, the new slots and whatever existing values its check covers), and no record is placed on a value the check did not exercise, so the eight untouched Codex values carry none. One convention across all three definitions: every value written or confirmed from a hands-on run says so the same way, so a later editor reads provenance identically in each host and the record is never a false claim about a value nobody checked. Roughly triples the record-keeping the sibling's form implies, and if that form is a repeatable script or per-value comment it must be produced and kept current for claude and codex too; how much of Claude Code it touches depends on the Existing Claude Code value scope question, and under a per-value form the hosts end up with some values carrying a record and others none, which a reader must not mistake for unchecked-equals-wrong.

Host coverage: all three checks are recorded. Form: the same form the Hands-on check record question settles for Antigravity. Value scope: for Claude Code and Codex the record attaches only to values the check changed (a new slot value whose wording the check rewrote, or an existing value the check contradicted); a value the claude or codex check merely confirmed as written carries no record, while every Antigravity value carries one since all of them are rewritten from the check. Keeps the record proportional to what the check actually decided: a Claude Code value lifted as written and confirmed gains nothing to maintain, while every value whose text the hands-on run determined is traceable the same way as the Antigravity ones. A confirmed value and an unchecked value look the same afterwards, so a later editor cannot tell whether a Claude Code or Codex value without a record was verified against the installed CLI or never looked at, which is exactly the ambiguity the record exists to remove; the changed/confirmed line also has to be judged per value during the checks.

Host coverage: all three checks are recorded. Form: the Antigravity check keeps whatever form the Hands-on check record question settles, while the claude and codex checks are each recorded in one lighter host-level note, independent of that form, naming the installed version checked, the date, and which slots and points (dispatch, waiting, continuing a finished agent, context file, or the Codex repair mechanics) the run covered. Every hands-on check leaves a trace a later editor can find, at a fraction of the Antigravity record's cost, matching the asymmetry in the decisions: Antigravity is rewritten wholesale from its check while Claude Code is kept as written unless contradicted and Codex re-checks only the repair mechanics. Two record conventions in one milestone, so a reader must know which host uses which and where each lives; a host-level note cannot say per value what was observed, and if the sibling settles on recording nowhere or on a form already lighter than this note, the asymmetry inverts or vanishes.

open-question.question: The definition loader gains refusals for a file-backed slot: a missing value file, a path outside the definition's slots/ subdirectory, and an entry that is neither a string nor a one-key file table. The build rendering test is decided as one full happy-path render. Do those refusals get their own pytest cases under the same interpreter-version skip, or is the happy-path render the only build test?
open-question.alternative: No refusal gets a pytest case in this milestone. The one full happy-path render is the build's only test, and the three new file-backed refusals (missing value file, path outside slots/, an entry that is neither a string nor a one-key file table) are checked only by reading the code and by trying them by hand while writing the loader. Refusal tests are never added as part of this milestone. A later milestone may add them if a regression shows up. Keeps the new build test as small as the rendering-test decision made it ("lightweight", one render). Adds no further synthetic definitions, and no refusal message gets pinned in a test that must change whenever its wording changes. The new code's error paths go untested, the path-containment check most of all, which is where an off-by-one in the is_inside-style comparison or a `..` escape would slip through. A later change to the slot loop could quietly turn a refusal into acceptance, or into an unhandled exception instead of a BuildError, and nothing in CI would notice.

The three new refusals get one pytest case each, in the rendering test's module under its module-level interpreter-version skip, so they are collected at the floor run and skipped there like the render. Each case writes a minimal synthetic definition directory into tmp_path whose settings.toml carries one bad slot entry: a `{ file }` table naming a file that is not there, one whose path resolves outside slots/, and one representative malformed entry (for example an integer). Each case calls load_definition directly and asserts a BuildError whose message names the slot and the refusal, rendering nothing. Existing slot refusals stay untested. Every new refusal is shown to fire, and to fire as the specific BuildError rather than some other failure, at the cost of three short cases that reuse the render test's skip and helpers. No build code changes, because load_definition already takes a directory. One sample per refusal leaves the boundary cases of the path check unexercised: an absolute path, a `..` escape, a path inside the definition directory but beside slots/. The malformed-entry refusal is also exercised by only one of its several shapes, so a bug in a shape the test does not try goes unseen.

Only the three new refusals are covered, in the rendering test's module under its skip, calling load_definition on a tmp_path synthetic definition and asserting the specific BuildError. Unlike the option above, the path and shape refusals are parametrized over their boundary variants. The path cases are a `..` escape, an absolute path, and a path inside the definition directory but outside slots/. The entry cases are a non-string scalar, a table with two keys, a one-key table whose key is not `file`, and a `file` value that is not a string. The missing-file case keeps one sample. Existing slot refusals stay untested. Exercises the places where containment and shape checks really go wrong. The path check is security-adjacent and the easiest of the three to get subtly wrong, and parametrizing keeps each variant to one line. Turns a lightweight test into a matrix of about eight cases for three refusals, with more synthetic setup to read and maintain. Some variants (absolute path, two-key table) may land on a refusal message shared with another variant, so their assertions duplicate one another.

alternative.id: All slot refusals one case each

open-question.alternative: Every refusal the slot-table loop raises gets one pytest case, in the rendering test's module under its skip, calling load_definition on a tmp_path synthetic definition and asserting the specific BuildError. That covers the three new file-backed refusals and also the existing ones: a name not matching the slot-name pattern, a reserved name (PLUGIN_ROOT, VERSION, NAME), a non-string, non-table value, and a value carrying a placeholder other than `{{PLUGIN_ROOT}}`, checked both inline and in a file-backed value. One sample is used per refusal. The milestone rewrites the slot loop that holds all of these checks, so testing the whole loop guards the existing refusals against being broken by the restructuring. The placeholder rule in particular must now also hold for file contents, and that is a new path through an old check. Widens the milestone's test scope to refusals that predate it and that no decision asked to cover. Roughly seven or eight cases pin that many message wordings, and the path-check boundaries are still only sampled once.

alternative.id: All slot refusals with boundary variants

open-question.alternative: Every refusal in the slot-table loop is covered, in the rendering test's module under its skip, by calling load_definition on a tmp_path synthetic definition and asserting the specific BuildError. The existing refusals (bad name, reserved name, wrong type, foreign placeholder inline and in a file) get one case each. The new path-outside and malformed-entry refusals are parametrized over their boundary variants (`..` escape, absolute path, path beside slots/; non-string scalar, two-key table, wrong key, non-string `file` value), and the missing file keeps one sample. The most complete guard on the rewritten slot loop. Both regressions in old checks and subtle errors in the new containment and shape checks surface in CI under the pinned run. The largest option: a dozen or more cases that make the refusal tests heavier than the one render they sit beside, against the goal's "lightweight" framing. It also has the widest set of pinned messages to keep in step with any rewording of the loader.
